deleted_rows.overview: Davis Peak is a steep, forested-then-rocky summit directly north of Gorge Lake in North Cascades National Park, just south of the Picket Range. Originally called Stetattle Peak, it was renamed in 1904 by the Reaburn survey party for the Davis family, early homesteaders who ran a roadhouse for trappers and travelers near present-day Diablo. The mountain is best known among climbers for its huge Northeast Face, which drops roughly 5,250 ft in one horizontal mile — one of the two steepest such drops in the contiguous U.S. The standard route climbs the peak's southwest side: a long, sustained, mostly off-trail approach gaining close to 6,000 ft, capped by a Class 3 (occasionally brief Class 4 on wet slab) scramble to the summit.
deleted_rows.beta: Two variants converge near the summit block: the classic South Ridge/South Buttress (Class 2-3, occasional Class 4 slab moves, with an exposed ~65° step-down at a notch below 5,800 ft on the old line) and the now-more-popular SW Face snow route (steepest snow ~40°+), which was pioneered as a ski descent and downgraded the peak to a 'non-technical' objective when snow-covered. Either way, the approach through the lower Gorge Creek forest — with cliff bands around 2,400 ft and 2,800 ft, dense alder/vine-maple, and (below ~4,000 ft on some lines) 2015-burn deadfall — is the real crux of the day.
deleted_rows.turnaround: Given the multi-thousand-foot, route-finding-heavy bushwhack approach and an equally long descent, set a firm turnaround time that guarantees clearing the brushy forest sections and any snow/rock scrambling before dark; do not push for the summit if you are already behind schedule on the approach.
deleted_rows.rock_grade: Class 3 with a few Class 4 moves (the forested bluffs low on the route)
deleted_rows.rappels: None. The party that climbed it in April 2026 carried a 30 m rope specifically for the forested bluffs, on the strength of other trip reports stressing the difficulty there, and never took it out of the pack — they cached it with the harnesses at the last rocky island before the snow. A short rope remains reasonable insurance for the bluffs and the one short vertical icy step on the upper face.
deleted_rows.comms: Assume no coverage. The route starts in the Skagit gorge at the Gorge Creek bridge and North Cascades National Park advises that cell service is limited or unavailable through its backcountry. Carry a satellite messenger or PLB. Newhalem and Diablo, the Seattle City Light company towns a few highway miles either side, are the nearest places to raise help by telephone; the Wilderness Information Center at Marblemount is the nearest staffed park facility.
deleted_rows.descent: Reverse the ascent route down the south ridge/buttress to the ~5,700 ft saddle and back down the Gorge Creek drainage. Stay well clear of the peak's Northeast side — its cliffs drop roughly 5,250 ft in one horizontal mile, among the most consequential terrain traps in the range if the party drifts off-route.

waypoints.name: Gorge Creek Overlook pull-off
waypoints.note: Parking pull-off on SR 20 near the Gorge Creek bridge, about 2.6 mi east of Newhalem; cross the highway bridge over Gorge Creek to start the off-trail ascent.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR-20 east from Newhalem about 2.6 miles to the Gorge Creek Overlook pull-off at the bridge. Nothing above the overlook is a numbered or maintained trail, and there is no reliable water past the lower forest, so fill up at Gorge Creek before starting.

waypoints.name: Lower cliff band
waypoints.note: First of two brushy cliff bands on the steep forest ascent; bypass on the right (south) side per the standard line.
waypoints.directions: Cross the footbridge over Gorge Creek, leave the overlook path immediately, and start straight up the forested south-southwest flank on boot-track, cairns and game trails. The lower forest is steep and brushy and partly inside a 2015 burn, so expect deadfall; an animal-path line through the open timber is generally the fastest way through. Near 2,400 ft the first cliff band blocks the fall line — work right around it.

waypoints.name: Upper cliff band
waypoints.note: Second cliff band above the first; stay right through mixed forest and brush to avoid exposed rock.
waypoints.directions: Above the first band the steep timber continues and the second cliff band arrives only about 400 ft higher. Work right again through mixed forest and brush rather than trying to force a line up the rock.

waypoints.name: Vine maple / open timber band
waypoints.note: Route opens into more travelable open timber with vine maple and occasional animal paths after the steep lower forest slog.
waypoints.directions: Keep grinding up steep timber to roughly 3,600-3,800 ft, where a brushy gully and intermittent animal paths lead into more open woods and the travel finally eases. This is the longest and least pleasant stretch of the day and there is no water on it.

waypoints.name: Snow-filled gully
waypoints.note: Partially snow-filled gully marking the transition from forest to the upper talus/snow terrain; can hold snow into midsummer.
waypoints.directions: A couple of hundred feet higher the forest gives out at a gully that commonly holds snow well into midsummer. Early season this is where the axe and crampons come out; later in the year it is bare and loose.

waypoints.name: Talus draw
waypoints.note: Narrow talus draw leading up into the alpine snowfields below the south ridge.
waypoints.directions: Follow the gully up into a narrow talus draw around 4,500 ft that leads clear of the trees. Granite slabs and alpine snowfields start around 4,800-4,850 ft and the angle eases as the ground flattens onto the crest of the southwest ridge.

waypoints.name: South Davis Saddle
waypoints.note: Broad saddle on the south ridge, about 4.4 hrs from the trailhead; flattest ground on the route for a break or bivy, and the gain point for the summit ridge/buttress.
waypoints.directions: Climb snow and talus up the crest to the broad saddle at about 5,700-5,800 ft. Stay left/north of Point 5,872, the subpeak on the east ridge — its slopes have turned parties back with avalanche-prone snow in shoulder-season conditions. Reckon on 4 to 4.5 hours from the car to here for a fit party.

waypoints.name: Davis Peak
waypoints.note: True summit via Class 2-3 rock buttress with slime-coated slabs near the top and a corniced south ridge crest just below.
waypoints.directions: From the saddle the inviting line is the wide-open snow slopes leading to the east summit ridge, and it is a trap: those slopes close out at an impassable step roughly 300 ft below the top, and the retreat costs hours and a thousand feet of regain. Take the rock buttress instead, climbing its right flank — it looks steep and loose from below but goes at Class 2-3. Near the top a short 3rd-class chimney and a band of mossy, slime-coated slabs are the last obstacle, and the slabs can be turned by traversing hard left. The south ridge crest just under the summit can carry a cornice.

deleted_rows.detailed_rack: This is a scramble, not a roped rock route, and most parties climb it with no rack at all. In early-season or winter conditions, when the south ridge/SW Face holds steep snow (up to roughly 60-65°), bring an ice axe and crampons; a short (30m) rope with a few slings and a picket or two can be useful for a running belay across a moat or for protecting the exposed step at the old south-ridge notch.
what_to_bring: gaiters and brush-resistant clothing for alder bushwhacking

deleted_rows.pro_needs: Class 2-3 scrambling on the approach and upper mountain, with brief Class 4 moves on wet or snow-covered slab reported by some parties near the top; no fixed rock protection is placed on the standard summer route. A helmet is worth carrying for the loose, broken terrain and for moat/cornice sections when snow lingers.
deleted_rows.best_season: Late spring is the easiest time: snow still covers much of the brush and snowmelt gives water on the way up. The route faces south almost the whole way, so mid-summer is very hot, and by late summer and fall the lack of water makes it an ordeal. It has also been climbed in winter during stable spells by strong, experienced parties.
deleted_rows.approach: From the Gorge Creek Overlook pull-off on Highway 20 (about 1,100 ft, roughly 2.6 miles/4.2 km east of Newhalem), cross the metal footbridge over Gorge Creek and immediately leave the maintained overlook trail — there is no numbered or maintained trail beyond the bridge, so the rest of the approach is off-trail route-finding by boot-track, cairns, and game trails up Davis Peak's south/southwest flank. The lower forest (partly within a 2015 burn) is steep and brushy with deadfall and blowdown; an animal-path line generally holds up through open timber. Around 2,400-2,800 ft, cliff bands force a bypass (parties generally work right); continue up steep timber to roughly 3,600-3,800 ft, where a brushy gully and intermittent animal paths lead through more open woods. Near 4,000 ft a partly snow-filled gully, and around 4,500 ft a talus draw, mark the transition out of forest; granite slabs and alpine snowfields begin around 4,800-4,850 ft, where the angle eases as the terrain flattens onto the crest of the southwest ridge. Stay left/north of Point 5,872 (a subpeak on Davis's east ridge, sometimes called "Little Davie," ~6,240 ft) rather than committing to its slopes - multiple parties have found avalanche-prone snow there in shoulder-season conditions and turned back - and climb snow/talus to the broad notch/saddle at roughly 5,700-5,800 ft on the south ridge (about 4-4.5 hours from the car for a fit party). There is no reliable water past the lower forest, so fill up at Gorge Creek near the trailhead. Total distance is roughly 6-8 miles round trip with about 5,900 ft of gain from trailhead to the 7,054 ft summit, almost all of it off-trail through brush, talus, and low-5th-class-adjacent terrain. A longer alternate approach follows the primitive Stetattle Creek Trail about 2 miles from Diablo, then leaves the trail, drops about 200 ft to ford Stetattle Creek, and climbs the peak's north/west side - but the Stetattle Creek Trail is fully closed by NPS due to 2023 Sourdough Fire damage (standing dead trees/debris), a long-term closure with no end date given on the park's fire-closures page updated September 14, 2026, so this alternate is not usable while it stands; plan on the Gorge Creek Overlook approach instead.
deleted_rows.descent_text: Descend the same southwest ridge/south buttress line back to the 5,700-5,800 ft saddle, then drop the forested southwest flank back toward Gorge Creek. This is fundamentally a walk-off/downclimb, not a rappel route - most parties, including at least one documented winter ascent, downclimb the entire way with careful footing rather than pulling out a rope; ropework is not standard on the summer scramble. That said, the upper south buttress has a short band of slime-coated, mossy slabs just below the summit ridge, plus a lower cliff band further down the buttress, that some parties choose to rappel instead of downclimb, especially when wet: expect at most one or two short, single-strand rappels (a 30-60 m rope is more than enough for either) off whatever natural anchor is available - a tree, horn, or sling around a block, as there are no bolted or fixed anchors reported anywhere on this route. Below the buttress, glissade or plunge-step the snow gully/talus draw back through about 4,500 ft, then descend the same brushy, deadfall-choked forest line (partly in the 2015 burn) through the cliff-band bypass around 2,400-2,800 ft and back down to the Gorge Creek footbridge and Highway 20. Watch footing on the steep forest sections (parties report significant knee strain) and stay off snow above Point 5,872 or the peak's steep east-facing terrain, which can carry cornices and avalanche hazard well into the season.
deleted_rows.bail: Retreat down the southwest slopes at most points.

pitch_detail.notes: From the ~5,700 ft South Davis Saddle (a little more than half a mile south of the summit), scramble up the right flank of the rock buttress; slime-coated slabs near the top are the reported crux.

itinerary.cal: Late May-June often gives firmer travel-friendly snow on the upper mountain than the bare, brushy summer approach, but requires ice axe/crampons and sometimes protection for moat crossings; check current trip reports for brush/burn-deadfall and snow conditions before committing to a start time.

access.fees: $10/person/night + a flat $6 nonrefundable reservation fee (charged mid-May–early Oct only; free the rest of the year). No separate climbing fee — North Cascades NP entrance itself is free.
access.notes: 60% of sites are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Leave No Trace; this is an off-trail route with no established campsites - camp on durable surfaces (rock, snow, or gravel) where possible. NPS backcountry rules require cross-country camping at least 1/2 mile from any maintained trail and out of sight of it. A permit is required only for overnight camping, not for a single-day scramble.
access.permit: No permit is needed for a day scramble. A NPS Wilderness Permit is required for overnight camping: reserve on Recreation.gov, watch the mandatory orientation video, then email noca_wilderness@nps.gov up to 3 days before the trip, or get a walk-up permit in person at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount. Summer-season (mid-May-early October) backcountry camping fees are $10 per person plus a $6 nonrefundable reservation fee (youth 15 and under free); no camping fee is charged early October-mid-May.
access.closures: SR 20 (North Cascades Highway) closes for the season in late November/early December and typically doesn't fully reopen until mid-to-late April (sometimes May in heavy-snow years) - check WSDOT's SR 20 pass report before driving. The Gorge Creek Overlook/Diablo trailhead area sits between the highway's two winter closure gates (Newhalem, milepost 120, and Ross Dam Trailhead/Silver Star, milepost 134/171), so it is among the first sections to lose road access as the highway closes and one of the last to reopen. The alternate Stetattle Creek Trail (the north/west approach via Diablo) is fully closed - not just historically closure-prone - due to standing dead trees and debris from the 2023 Sourdough Fire; NPS lists the entire trail as a long-term closure, with no end date given, on its fire-closures page updated September 14, 2026. Do not plan on this alternate approach until NPS lifts the closure; use the standard Gorge Creek Overlook approach instead.
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)
access.passRequired: None. Davis Peak's trailheads (Gorge Creek Overlook, Stetattle Creek/Diablo) are within North Cascades National Park/Ross Lake National Recreation Area, which charges no entrance fee and requires no day-use parking pass. A Northwest Forest Pass is only needed at trailheads on adjacent national forest land elsewhere along SR 20 (e.g., Rainy Lake, Blue Lake near Washington Pass) - not at this trailhead.

approach_variants.name: Gorge Creek: straight up, and the 3,800 ft vine maples
approach_variants.notes: From the Gorge Creek Overlook parking area near 1,100 ft, cross the footbridge and start climbing essentially straight up the slope above; the bearing is unsubtle and the line is narrow. The first thousand feet is the slowest of the day — fallen timber stacked like pick-up-sticks, young trees and burnt charcoal from the fire that ran through here — and can take an hour on its own. Cliff bands come at about 2,400 ft and again at about 2,800 ft and are bypassed on the right. Above them a network of animal paths climbs a slight ridge feature through open timber, which is the sign you are past both. Fill up at Gorge Creek: there is no reliable water above the lower forest.
hazards: Dense blowdown and burnt deadfall in the lower forest; deviating even a short way off the line puts you in far worse brush
Two cliff bands below 3,000 ft
Avalanche-prone snow on the slopes around Point 5,872 in shoulder-season conditions
Wet, slime-coated slabs near the summit
approach_variants.baseFinding: The ladder of four markers, then a hard left under the slabs. From about 3,800 ft the route works left through vine maples to a partially snow-filled gully at roughly 4,000 ft; that gully leads to a tiny talus draw at about 4,500 ft, then to alpine snowfields near 4,800 ft, and the ground first looks promising at granite slabs around 4,850 ft, where the angle eases onto the southwest ridge crest. Take those four in order — vine maple, snow gully, tiny talus draw, granite slabs — and you are on the line. Stay left and north of Point 5,872 rather than committing to its slopes; parties have found avalanche-prone snow there and turned back, and the bump beyond it on the east ridge is a false summit, not Davis. At the top the buttress that looks steep and loose is reasonable Class 2-3 except for slime-coated slabs near the summit: the instruction is a hard leftward traverse, resisting the temptation to scramble the slabs. If you are on wet slab, you are off route.

bivy.name: Gorge Creek overlook, the trailhead you sleep at
bivy.notes: This is where the standard scramble starts, on Highway 20 between Newhalem and Diablo. You cross the creek on the bridge and go straight into steep forest with no trail of any kind. The peak is famous for the sheer drop off its far side, and the ground you climb reflects that: expect around ten miles and roughly seven and a half thousand feet of gain, with cliff bands to be turned in the timber around twenty-four hundred and twenty-eight hundred feet and a stretch of vine maple higher. Thirteen or fourteen hours car to car is a normal time for a fit party, and that is why so many sleep at the car rather than carry overnight gear up it. Being west of the seasonal highway gate, the pullout is reachable all year, but the route wants firm snow or dry ground rather than the rotten mix in between.
bivy.water: Gorge Creek itself, immediately below, and it is the last certain water for a long way up. Nothing is provided at the pullout.
bivy.permit: No permit and no fee to park or to sleep in a vehicle. A DAY climb from here needs no backcountry permit at all, which is the usual way this peak is done. The moment you sleep on the mountain you need a National Park Service backcountry permit for the Davis Peak cross-country zone.
bivy.capacity: A highway pullout and viewpoint parking area, not a campground. Parties routinely spend the night in a vehicle here to start at first light. There are no sites, no pitches, and nowhere to put a tent.

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, Newhalem
bivy.notes: About five minutes' drive west of the Gorge Creek overlook, this is the practical base for a party that wants a real campsite the night before rather than a night in the driver's seat. It is low, forested and close to the highway, with none of the character of the alpine above it, and that is fine for its purpose. It also stays open later in the year than the larger campgrounds nearby, which matters on a peak whose best conditions are often outside the busy season. The obvious closer option is gone: the small tent campground at Gorge Lake, right beside the creek in Diablo, has been shut for an extended period over debris-flow and flooding hazard on ground burned in an earlier fire, and should not be planned around without confirming it has reopened.
bivy.water: Potable water while the campground is serviced; the river is the fallback and needs treating. Availability drops off outside the main season.
bivy.permit: National Park Service, Ross Lake NRA. No backcountry permit needed to sleep here. It has historically been the free, year-round, minimal-service option in the Newhalem cluster while the fee campgrounds close for winter — confirm the current fee and season, because the park has been adjusting both.
bivy.capacity: A modest road campground on the Skagit with a mix of standard sites and a couple of group sites, small enough that a busy summer weekend fills it.

bivy.name: Snowfield benches on the south side, around 4,800 feet
bivy.notes: The forest below is the whole difficulty of this mountain — steep, tangled and unrelenting, with the route picked out along animal paths and through weaknesses in the cliff bands. Getting up to this level and stopping turns a punishing single day into a manageable two, and this is the first ground on the route where a party can lie flat and see out. A partly snow-filled gully around four thousand feet is the usual way through the last of the trees onto these slopes; it is straightforward when it holds firm snow and considerably less pleasant when it is running wet or bare. Early summer is the moment for this camp, because the same snow that makes the gully work is what supplies the water.
bivy.water: Running snowmelt while there is snow, which is exactly what makes this level worth stopping at. Once the slopes bare out later in summer, water here becomes unreliable and the gully lower down is the last dependable source.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required for the Davis Peak cross-country zone: six people maximum in a party, and a maximum of three parties in the zone on any night. Walk-up only, collected in person at the Marblemount wilderness office rather than reserved in advance. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground and not in meadow or within a hundred feet of water. No fires anywhere in the zone. Pack waste out where the ground will not take a cathole.
bivy.capacity: Open ground rather than sites. Where the timber finally releases into alpine snow and slabs there is room for a small party to lie down, and no established platform to aim for.

bivy.name: The 5,720 ft saddle south of the summit
bivy.notes: A little over half a mile south of the summit, this notch in the ridge is the highest sensible sleeping ground on the peak and the launching point for the last of the climbing. From here the standard finish takes the rock buttress on the south ridge at easy scrambling, a couple of grades of hands-on ground rather than anything technical. Parties have also tried the broad snow slopes of the east ridge from the saddle and been stopped by a step a few hundred feet under the top, so the south side is the line to plan for. Being a saddle it is exposed to whatever the weather is doing and there is nothing to shelter behind, which argues for using it on a settled forecast and otherwise sleeping lower. Note the other approach: the peak's steep north-east side is reached instead from the Stetattle Creek trail out of Diablo, leaving the path after a couple of miles and fording the creek — but that trail has been closed outright for falling dead trees on burned ground, so treat the Gorge Creek side as the only way in until it reopens.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, and only while snow is present at the notch. Late in a dry summer there is nothing here and everything has to be carried up from the snowfields below.
bivy.permit: Same National Park Service backcountry permit and Davis Peak cross-country zone as the ground below: party of six maximum, three parties per night, walk-up from Marblemount, no fires, durable surfaces only.

deleted_rows.overview: A less-common, longer glacier approach to Little Tahoma from Paradise, crossing the Paradise, Cowlitz, and Ingraham glaciers past the Cathedral Rocks cleaver to reach the peak's south/east face, finishing up a gully-chimney and a short exposed scramble to the summit. deleted_rows.beta: From Paradise, follow the standard Camp Muir route to about 8,600 ft, then traverse northeast across the Paradise and Cowlitz glaciers (staying at elevation, avoiding a serac/cliff band below), through a notch in the Cathedral Rocks cleaver, and across the Ingraham Glacier to a snow/rock ramp at the base of Little Tahoma's south/east face (~8,900 ft). deleted_rows.turnaround: Set a turnaround time before departure given the serac/crevasse exposure on the traverse and the avalanche/wind-slab risk on the summit ramp, and commit to it rather than push late.

deleted_rows.descent: Reverse the ascent: down the gully/scramble, back across the Ingraham, Cowlitz, and Paradise glaciers, and down the Camp Muir route to Paradise.

waypoints.name: Little Tahoma Peak summit
waypoints.directions: Climb the Camp Muir route from Paradise to about 8,600 ft, below Anvil Rock, then rope up and traverse east across the Paradise and Cowlitz glaciers, holding elevation above the cliff and serac band, through the notch in the Cathedral Rocks cleaver, and across the Ingraham to the ramp at the base of the face near 8,900 ft. Above, climb a loose gully, a short step and a gully-chimney to the summit notch, then scramble the exposed crest to the summit.

deleted_rows.detailed_rack: Glacier travel kit (rope, pickets, crevasse rescue gear, ice axe, crampons) plus a light rock rack (a few cams/nuts and slings) for the low 5th-class pitches and final scramble.

Winter camping gear if bivying on the glacier/cleaver
pro_tips: Stay at consistent elevation (~8,600 ft) crossing the Cowlitz/Ingraham glaciers rather than dropping toward the cliff/serac band below.
Move quickly under any active serac zones on the Cowlitz/Ingraham traverse.
The summit ramp can be a wind slab in early season — assess it carefully before committing.
watch_out: A known no-fall-zone exists on the Cowlitz Glacier traverse beneath seracs — move efficiently through it.
The final ridge-crest scramble to the summit is loose and exposed.
Route becomes substantially more hazardous once the glaciers open up later in spring/summer.
deleted_rows.pro_needs: Crevasse rescue protection for the long glacier traverse, plus light rock protection for the short low-5th-class sections near the summit.
deleted_rows.best_season: Best attempted winter through early spring, when the Cowlitz and Ingraham glaciers are more consolidated; by late spring/summer the glaciers become significantly more broken and hazardous to cross, which is why most parties use the Frying Pan/Whitman (East Shoulder) route instead once the White River Road opens.
deleted_rows.approach: From the Paradise parking lot, climb the standard Camp Muir route to about 8,600 ft, then traverse east onto the Paradise Glacier and across the Cowlitz Glacier (maintaining elevation, avoiding the cliff/serac band below), through a notch in the Cathedral Rocks cleaver, and across the Ingraham Glacier to a snow or rock ramp at the base of Little Tahoma's south/east face (~8,900 ft). Camp is commonly made on the Cowlitz or Ingraham glacier, or on the more exposed Cathedral Rocks cleaver.
deleted_rows.descent_text: Down-climb the summit scramble and gully-chimney, re-rope for the Ingraham/Cowlitz/Paradise glacier crossing (retracing the same line through the Cathedral Rocks notch), then descend the standard Camp Muir/Paradise route; skiing is possible only off the east face and near Anvil Rock for parties equipped to do so.
deleted_rows.bail: Retreat back across the Ingraham/Cowlitz/Paradise glaciers toward Camp Muir and Paradise; the Cathedral Rocks notch and the traverse below the serac/cliff band are the key sections to clear before deteriorating weather or snow conditions.

pitch_detail.notes: Leave the Camp Muir route below Anvil Rock and traverse east across the Paradise and Cowlitz glaciers, holding about 8,600 ft to stay above the cliff and serac band below. Pass through the obvious notch in the Cathedral Rocks cleaver and cross the Ingraham Glacier toward the snow or rock ramp at the base of the face (~8,900 ft). Best in winter to early spring; the glaciers get more dangerous later.
pitch_detail.pitch: Cowlitz/Ingraham glacier traverse to south face base

pitch_detail.notes: Gain the saddle between the Ingraham and Whitman glaciers by a steep snow couloir, topped by a short scramble up loose rock with a Class 4 move or two. Knock nothing down on your own party in the couloir.

Climb the Whitman Glacier above toward the summit block and leave it at its upper left-hand corner, entering the gully that splits the summit rocks. Sun cups can be deep on the upper glacier by early summer.
pitch_detail.pitch: Upper Whitman Glacier corner into gully

pitch_detail.notes: Climb about two-thirds of the way up the gully to a short step at a headwall. The rock is loose throughout; keep the party close together so any rock knocked loose has little room to gain speed.
A short, steep step blocks the gully at the headwall. Climb it directly; a light rock rack is useful here and for the summit scramble if the party wants protection.
Above the step, continue up a gully that narrows into a chimney and ends at the notch below the summit. Loose and sometimes mixed with snow or ice early in the season.

From the notch make a short, loose and very exposed scramble along the ridge crest to the true summit (11,138 ft); the summit block has two rock horns separated by a shallow gully. Down-climb the same way with care.

deleted_rows.itinerary: Typically a 2-day trip: Day 1, approach from Paradise to a camp on the Cowlitz/Ingraham glacier or Cathedral Rocks cleaver (6-8 hrs); Day 2, climb from camp to the summit (4-6 hrs) and descend to Paradise. Can be done as a single long day in ideal conditions.

approach_variants.name: Paradise and the Muir route to 8,600 ft, then east through the Cathedral Rocks notch
approach_variants.notes:
From the Paradise parking lot, climb the standard Camp Muir route to about 8,600 ft. Leave it there and traverse east onto the Paradise Glacier and across the Cowlitz, holding elevation to stay above the cliff and serac band below, then through a notch in the Cathedral Rocks cleaver and across the Ingraham Glacier to a snow or rock ramp at the base of Little Tahoma's south and east face near 8,900 ft.

Camps are made on the Cowlitz or Ingraham glaciers, or on the more exposed Cathedral Rocks cleaver.

Above the ramp the route climbs the Whitman Glacier and exits its upper left-hand corner into a gully, climbs about two-thirds of it to a short step, continues up a gully-chimney to the summit notch, and finishes with a short loose scramble along the crest.

The Paradise road stays open far later into winter than the roads on the north and east sides, which is the whole reason this variant exists.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Nov-May. This is the winter and early-spring line, used precisely when the White River road to Summerland is shut and the Fryingpan approach is unavailable
hazards: Serac fall and crevasse hazard across an extended Cowlitz and Ingraham traverse
A cliff and serac band immediately below the traverse line, which is why elevation must be held
Wind-slab avalanche potential on the ramp gaining the face in early season
Loose rock in the summit gully-chimney and on the final crest scramble
A long committing traverse with the same ground to reverse on the way out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The decision is at 8,600 ft and it is a leaving, not an arriving. You step off the Camp Muir track while still about 1,500 ft below Camp Muir. If you reach Camp Muir you have gone too far — by a vertical quarter of a mile, on the busiest bootpack on the mountain, which is exactly why it happens.

Count what you cross: three glaciers and one rock cleaver, in this order — Paradise, Cowlitz, then a notch in Cathedral Rocks, then the Ingraham. If you have crossed the Cowlitz and walked into rock without finding a notch, you are below the notch and need to regain height. The traverse deliberately holds elevation to stay above a serac and cliff band; drifting down is the error that feels easy at the time.

The base is a ramp, and it is the only ramp: a snow or rock ramp at about 8,900 ft leading onto the south and east face. Arriving at the foot of a face with no ramp means you are round the wrong side of it.

The negative that separates this from the peak's other route: the standard line on Little Tahoma comes from the Fryingpan side, over Whitman Notch, from the east. This one comes from Paradise, from the southwest, and never goes near Summerland or Meany Crest.

Why this route exists and when it stops working: it is the winter line, done before the Cowlitz and Ingraham become too broken to cross safely. Once those glaciers open up, the traverse is the hazard rather than the climb.

deleted_rows.fa: Fred Berry and Lawrence Buchanan, 1936 (first ascent of the peak)

deleted_rows.overview: Whatcom Peak stands guard at the northwest gateway to the Picket Range above Whatcom Pass, one of the more accessible summits in a range known for brutal approaches. This Southwest/Whatcom Glacier line is the standard way to combine Whatcom Peak with neighboring Mount Challenger. Like most Picket Range glaciers, the Whatcom Glacier has thinned noticeably in recent years — parties recently describe sections of bare ice and a badly deteriorated summit notch by late summer, so do not assume conditions are what they were in past years.
deleted_rows.beta: From Whatcom Pass the standard approach descends on a traversing line to about 5,200 ft to round the base of Whatcom Peak's NW rib, then crosses polished slabs below the Whatcom Glacier on the peak's east side to reach Perfect Pass at the south side of the mountain. From Perfect Pass the summit is 'an easy grab' — a snow slope of moderate angle followed by a short but exposed Class 3 ridge scramble to the higher, northeast summit point. The Whatcom Glacier is shrinking quickly and can present bare ice and shallow crevasses in late season, so many parties treat the crossing as roped glacier travel. This route is also reachable/exited via Easy Ridge and 'Imperfect Impasse' from the Chilliwack side, or combined with an ascent of Mount Challenger from Perfect Pass.
deleted_rows.turnaround: Set a turnaround time that leaves enough daylight and weather margin to re-cross the Whatcom Glacier traverse and descend to Whatcom Pass before conditions deteriorate — the glacier crossing and exposed summit ridge are markedly more hazardous in poor visibility, on softened afternoon snow, or after refreeze turns slopes to hard ice.
deleted_rows.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
deleted_rows.comms: No reliable cell service is expected anywhere along this remote North Cascades National Park route; carry a satellite communicator or PLB for emergency contact.
deleted_rows.descent: Descend via the standard descent route, retracing the ascent when possible. Be aware of loose rock and snow bridge hazards. Maintain group cohesion on exposed sections.

deleted_rows.detailed_rack: A light glacier-travel and scrambling kit rather than a rock rack: a rope for the Whatcom Glacier crossing, crevasse-rescue hardware (pulleys, prusiks or mechanical ascenders, spare slings/cord), ice axe and crampons for the glacier slabs and summit snow slope, and a helmet for the exposed Class 3 ridge.

deleted_rows.pro_needs: Protection needs are minimal since this is a glacier-travel and scramble route rather than a roped rock climb, but a rope, pickets as conditions dictate, and a full crevasse-rescue kit are essential for the Whatcom Glacier crossing.
deleted_rows.approach: From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead (~3,100 ft, at the end of Ruth Creek Rd/FR 32 off the Mt. Baker Highway) follow the Hannegan Pass Trail (#674) 4.2-4.6 miles and about 2,000 ft of gain, alongside Ruth Creek through forest and subalpine meadows, to Hannegan Pass (5,066 ft) — the last easy, reliable water before dropping into North Cascades National Park. From the pass, descend the Chilliwack River Trail through long, viewless switchbacks (losing roughly 2,800 ft) to the Chilliwack River valley, passing Boundary/Copper Creek camps; the river itself is crossed via a hand-pulled cable car near US Cabin Camp rather than a ford. Continue up-valley on the Brush Creek Trail toward Graybeal Camp — roughly 14 trail miles and a cumulative ~4,400 ft of gain from the trailhead to this point — and note that the small creek near Graybeal is unreliable and can run dry by late summer, so fill up earlier at the Chilliwack River or US Cabin Camp. Past Graybeal the maintained tread gives way to a steep, brushy, root-and-timber climbers' path that gains roughly 2,000 ft over the final 3 miles to Whatcom Pass (5,206 ft), passing Whatcom Camp, an established backcountry site with the first real views of the Challenger Glacier. From Whatcom Pass, leave the trail and climb/contour south and east to gain the Whatcom Glacier at roughly 5,200-5,500 ft; rope up for glacier travel toward Perfect Pass, the notch/saddle south of the peak — crevasses and moats open through the season, and the surface can go from soft névé early on to bare, polished ice with exposed water channels by mid-to-late summer. From the glacier's high point near Perfect Pass, ascend the broad south-facing snowfield below the summit and finish on an exposed but moderate Class 3 scramble along the south ridge crest to the top. Water is available at Ruth Creek near the trailhead and at the Chilliwack River; treat the cable-car river crossing, the brushy unmaintained climbers' trail above Graybeal, and crevasse/moat navigation on the glacier as the main hazards of the approach.
deleted_rows.descent_text: This is a walk-off/downclimb — there is no rappelling on this route. From the summit, reverse the exposed Class 3 south-ridge scramble down to the top of the south snowfield, then descend the snowfield back onto the Whatcom Glacier at roughly 5,200-5,500 ft. Rope back up for glacier travel and reverse the traverse across the east/south side of the peak toward Perfect Pass and back to Whatcom Pass; crevasses and moats are typically more open on the descent as the afternoon sun softens the snowpack, so budget time for careful navigation rather than a quick glissade — the glacier can deteriorate to bare ice with gaping moats later in the season. From Whatcom Pass, descend the same trail system used on approach: the climbers' path down to Graybeal Camp, the Brush Creek/Chilliwack River Trail back to the cable-car crossing of the Chilliwack River, then back up and over Hannegan Pass and down the Hannegan Pass Trail to the trailhead. Given the roughly 17+ trail miles one-way just to reach Whatcom Pass, most parties camp near Perfect Pass (Graybeal and Whatcom Camp are closed until further notice after fire damage) and treat this as a multi-day trip rather than a car-to-car push, descending only as far as the next camp on summit day. If the summit notch is badly melted out and choss-prone, an alternate descent drops about 200 ft north of Peak 7347 to reach the Wiley Glacier instead of reversing through the notch.

approach_variants.notes:
From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at about 3,100 ft at the end of Ruth Creek Road, FR-32, off the Mt. Baker Highway, Trail #674 runs 4.2-4.6 miles and about 2,000 ft alongside Ruth Creek to Hannegan Pass at 5,066 ft, the last easy reliable water before dropping into the national park.

From the pass, descend the Chilliwack River Trail through long viewless switchbacks, losing roughly 2,800 ft, past Boundary and Copper Creek camps. The river is crossed via a hand-pulled cable car near US Cabin Camp rather than a ford, which is the practical difference between this and the Easy Ridge approach.

Continue up-valley on the Brush Creek Trail toward Graybeal Camp, roughly 14 trail miles and a cumulative 4,400 ft of gain from the trailhead. The small creek near Graybeal is unreliable and can run dry by late summer, so fill earlier at the Chilliwack or US Cabin Camp. Past Graybeal the maintained tread gives way to a steep, brushy, root-and-timber climbers' path gaining roughly 2,000 ft over the final 3 miles to Whatcom Pass at 5,206 ft, passing Whatcom Camp and the first real views of the Challenger Glacier.

approach_variants.baseFinding:
This route's own ground is the glacier, and you are on it as soon as you leave Whatcom Pass. From the pass, leave the trail and climb and contour south and east to gain the Whatcom Glacier at roughly 5,200-5,500 ft, then rope up and travel toward Perfect Pass, the notch and saddle south of the peak.

So the discriminator against the other two routes on this peak is the first move out of Whatcom Pass, and it is three-way: south and up the crest is the North Ridge. South and east onto ice at 5,200-5,500 ft is this route. Nothing from Whatcom Pass is the South Spur, which is approached from Easy Ridge on the other side.

Arrival at the climbing proper: from the glacier's high point near Perfect Pass, the route ascends the broad south-facing snowfield below the summit and finishes on an exposed but moderate class 3 scramble along the south ridge crest. The snowfield is the same one the South Spur uses. The two routes share their last hour and differ entirely in everything before it.

What the glacier does through the season, which is the real variable: crevasses and moats open as the year goes on and the surface can go from soft neve early to bare, polished ice with exposed water channels by mid to late summer. On the descent they are typically more open than on the way up as the afternoon sun softens the snowpack, so budget time for careful navigation rather than a quick glissade.

An alternate exit worth knowing before you need it: if the summit notch is badly melted out and choss-prone, a descent drops about 200 ft north of Peak 7347 to reach the Wiley Glacier instead of reversing through the notch.

It is reached either over Whatcom Pass from the Brush Creek side or along Easy Ridge, the latter demanding a substantial descent and reclimb to get around the gap short of the pass. Parties coming that way typically chain Boundary, Copper Creek or US Cabin, then Graybeal on Brush Creek, then here — three or four days of walking before any climbing begins. deleted_rows.approach: This is the same Northwest Shoulder line to High Pass and the Whitehorse (So-Bahli-Ahli) Glacier — same Niederprum Trailhead, same Moose Creek bridge barricade detour, same Trail #653 to 'the flat,' same couloir to Lone Tree Pass, same traverse to High Pass — climbed specifically as an early-season snow/ice ascent rather than the late-season rock-and-snow scramble. The distinction is timing and line choice, not trailhead: parties doing this variant go earlier (roughly April–June) while the couloirs, glacier basin, and connecting slopes are still fully snow-covered corn/neve, and they tend to stay on continuous snow/ice higher on the shoulder and face rather than threading rock bands that appear once the snowpack recedes. It's a popular ski-mountaineering objective in this window — many parties skin/boot the glacier basin on skis or splitboards and switch to crampons only for the final steep pitch below the summit. Because of the earlier timing, expect firmer early-morning snow requiring a timed start, and real avalanche hazard in the entry couloir and on the glacier headwall that isn't a factor once the route melts out later in the year; check the NWAC forecast and go when the freeze-thaw cycle is consolidating the snowpack, not loading it. For this early-season snow/ice ascent, some parties instead follow a more direct line via Snow Gulch: from the Niederprum trailhead area, follow the old forest-road grade toward Snow Gulch, then ascend the creek drainage through a steep bushwhack section (roughly 1,100-2,200 ft, via slide alder or adjacent slabs) that only makes sense once deep snow has buried the brush; many parties stash skis/boards around 2,500 ft in the old growth for the descent.
deleted_rows.descent_text: Reverse the ascent. In good early-season corn-snow conditions this is where the route earns its ski-mountaineering reputation: strong parties descend on skis or splitboards from as close to the summit as conditions allow, riding the upper face/shoulder snow, the glacier basin, and the connecting slopes back toward High Pass and Lone Tree Pass before booting or hiking out the lower couloir and Niederprum Trail once snow cover thins. The same summit bergschrund/moat obstacle found on the standard route is still there — whether it requires a rappel depends heavily on how well it's bridged that season. Earlier in the season (which is when this ice/snow variant is typically climbed) the schrund is more often snow-covered and can sometimes be downclimbed or skied past directly; if it's open, treat it exactly as on the standard Northwest Shoulder — expect one rappel (occasionally two) off a natural anchor (slung rock horn or old fixed piton, both of which should be backed up or replaced), using a doubled 30 m or single 60 m rope. Below the schrund, continue the reversal down the glacier and couloirs to Lone Tree Pass and out the Niederprum Trail. Because this is a long, remote, snow-condition-dependent descent, carry an avalanche kit and pick your descent window (corn cycle) as carefully as the ascent.
deleted_rows.bail: Retreat down the glacier the way you came; the steep icy rollover and crevassed glacier sections are the most serious to downclimb if conditions deteriorate (softening snow, whiteout, or new snowfall raising avalanche risk) — don't push past the rollover if you're not confident retreating through it.

approach_variants.name: Lone Tree Pass and High Pass, early season
approach_variants.notes: Park at the steel gate and boulder barricade where the road is closed at the washed-out creek bridge and walk the old mining-road grade south. The standard line climbs to the sloping bench by the old mine workings, marked by a large broken silvered snag, then makes a rising leftward traverse to Lone Tree Pass, with the broad snow platform just beyond it serving as the high camp. From there traverse to High Pass at the top of the broad snow couloir below the prominent point to its north, and step onto the glacier. Climbed early in the season some parties instead take the more direct Snow Gulch line up the creek drainage, which only makes sense once deep snow has buried the slide alder; skis are commonly stashed around 2,500 ft in the old growth for the descent.

approach_variants.baseFinding: High Pass is the entry to the glacier and the summit block above it is the base of the climbing proper. Come over Lone Tree Pass, make the long rising traverse to High Pass at the top of the broad snow couloir beneath the prominent point north of it, and step onto the glacier there. Climbed at this time of year the whole basin is continuous snow, so the marker is not a rock feature: the proof that you are at the foot of the final pitch is a large bergschrund running right around the perimeter of the summit block, visible from well down the glacier. Above it the ground steepens to roughly 50 degrees and can be firm neve or bare ice, and it is where parties stash skis and go to crampons. If you are still on low-angle, skinnable glacier with no schrund across your line, you are below the summit block. If you are threading open crevasses and bare ice rather than moving on continuous snow, you are here too late in the year for this variation and should be on the melted-out rock-and-snow line instead.

climbing_route.label: Continuous snow/ice on the shoulder and face
climbing_route.notes: Climbed roughly April–June as an early-season snow/ice ascent while the couloirs, glacier basin, and connecting slopes are still fully snow-covered corn/névé; parties stay on continuous snow/ice higher on the shoulder and face rather than threading the rock bands that appear once the snowpack recedes. Many skin/boot the glacier basin on skis or splitboards. Expect firmer early-morning snow requiring a timed start, and real avalanche hazard in the entry couloir and on the glacier headwall that isn't a factor once the route melts out later in the year — check the NWAC forecast and go when the freeze-thaw cycle is consolidating the snowpack, not loading it.

climbing_route.label: Final steep pitch below the summit
climbing_route.notes: Parties switch to crampons only for the final steep pitch below the summit.

bivy.name: Whitehorse high camp, benches near Lone Tree Pass
bivy.notes: This is the high camp for the Northwest Shoulder, and most parties who do not intend a twelve-to-sixteen hour car-to-car day use it. The route is around 6,000 to 7,000 feet of gain from a low trailhead and the lower trail is notoriously steep and brushy, so splitting it at the pass converts a punishing single day into two reasonable ones and puts the glacier and the exposed summit scrambling in the morning. The sheltered meadow just beyond the pass is the pick — trees break the wind and it looks straight at the summit. Everything about this approach depends on the Mine Road out of the highway west of Darrington: it is rough, narrow, overgrown enough to scratch a vehicle, and has had bridge and washout closures that push the start well down the hill and add road walking. Confirm how far you can drive before you plan the day. Early season with snow cover over the brush is much the better time; by late summer the glacier above develops crevasses and a large bergschrund and the brush below is at its worst.
bivy.water: Snowmelt in season and the small tarn below the pass on the traverse east; both are seasonal. By late summer this side dries out and there may be nothing, so carry up or plan to melt. There is no water on the trail below.
bivy.permit: Boulder River Wilderness — no permit to camp, no quota, no self-issue box. No fee at the trailhead, which is unusual for this area and reflects how minimal the parking is. Fires are a bad idea on this ground and are commonly banned outright in late summer.
bivy.capacity: Informal — a flat sheltered meadow just past the pass takes a couple of tents, with smaller pockets on benches nearby and more ground on the traverse east toward the small lake below the pass. One or two parties.

bivy.name: Whitehorse Community Park campground, Darrington
bivy.notes: The nearest developed drive-in base to the Mine Road, sitting just outside Darrington with the mountain itself directly in view, which makes it a useful place to look at conditions on the northwest side the evening before. Its real role is staging: the Niederprum trailhead has room for only a handful of vehicles and nothing else, so sleeping in town and driving up in the small hours is the usual pattern rather than camping at the road end. Because it is county-run its season and fees are set separately from the forest campgrounds and change independently of them. The winter closure is the catch — the best window for the Northwest Shoulder is spring, and the campground may not be open yet.
bivy.water: Developed park water in season; confirm before relying on it outside summer
bivy.permit: County park, not national forest — a nightly fee applies and no federal or state pass does anything here. Seasonal: closed and winterized through the winter months, roughly mid-autumn to mid-spring, which rules it out for the spring snow season when Whitehorse is actually in condition.

approach_variants.baseFinding:
From Pinnacle Saddle you go east. Plummer Peak is west, and the boot paths fork at the saddle, so this is a decision and not a default.

The base is defined by two objects and the relationship between them: a western prominence, and an obvious chute immediately east of it. About a quarter mile of boot path from the saddle. If you cannot identify a prominence, you cannot identify the chute — go on until you can see one, rather than starting up the first weakness.

The positive test is counter-intuitive, which is why it is worth carrying: the correct chute gets better as it gets steeper. The lower approach is scree and choss; the chute itself is progressively steeper and progressively better-cleaned rock. So if the rock is getting looser as you climb, you are in the wrong gully. That is the reverse of what most loose volcanic scrambles do, and it is the most reliable signal on this route.

Stay on the most-travelled line on the approach scree. There are multiple possible lines; the worst loose rock is off the beaten one.

A clean negative about hardware: there is no fixed protection anywhere on this route. Only natural options exist — a few horns and trees near the top that can be slung. If you find bolts, a piton, or a fixed station, you are on one of the peak's roped lines, not on the scramble. The East Ridge, in particular, has an old piton and a fixed rappel anchor.

Downclimb planning as part of the finding: the class 4 section is more hazardous in descent than ascent because the rock is loose. Parties who intend to back off do it with an improvised sling on a horn or a tree near the top — worth spotting one on the way up.

wa_davis_peak_nc_south_slope_and_ridge.beta:
Almost all the difficulty here is brush, steepness and route-finding rather than climbing. The rock is rated Class 4, but that grade comes from a January ascent, when good snow may have covered the harder steps; the bare-rock difficulty and the number of pitches, if any, are not known.

From the Gorge Creek bridge at 1,096 ft the slope is sustained from the first step, gaining roughly 1,800 ft in the first half mile through small evergreens with a salal and brush understory. There is no trail, and numerous rock outcrops make navigation important. One recorded line: from near the highway curve, hike due north to about 2,800 ft, turn northeast and ascend to the 4,920+ ft point, then go straight uphill on a bearing of about 340 degrees true to Point 5872, where the south ridge becomes obvious. A party approaching via Gorge Creek instead took the South Buttress, turning cliff bands at about 2,400 ft and 2,800 ft on the right, moving through open timber and alpine snowfields, and reaching the South Davis saddle at 5,700 ft in 4.4 hours from the car; they described Class 2-3 scrambling on the buttress with slime-coated rock slabs near the top. A third account has the granite slabs starting around 4,850 ft after a brushy gully at 3,600 ft, bypassing Point 5872 to the north, and reaching a south-ridge viewpoint at 6,300 ft.

From the 5,720+ ft saddle, climb 200 ft of slab to the sharp ridge that leads to the summit. In good snow this is step-kicking; bare it is class 4 slab. In snow this is where the route's steepest ground is — the notch on the old standard south ridge line is reported at 65 degrees, which is precisely why skiers pushed a variation onto the southwest face. Above it the crest broadens into an almost level, wide-open ridge to the summit, one of the great walkable viewpoints in the range and simultaneously the top of the largest cornices most people will ever stand near. In summer that broad snow crest may instead be a scramble among rocks with steep drops on both sides.

There is also a variation that its climber did not rate: from the saddle, drop east into the basin under the east side of the south ridge, traverse up and north as far as possible, then turn west and climb beside the cliff edge. The turn involves a ten-foot step that looked trivial and was not — iced-in cracks and wrong-feeling holds, passed with ice-axe belays. The direct ridge, descended on the return, offered every ledge needed to get down. Take the ridge.
watch_out: The summit ridge is corniced along its entire length above the northeast face; in winter you are walking on the roof of the largest cornices in the area.
Rock outcrops and cliff bands riddle the lower slope. Getting them wrong on descent means rappelling off trees.
Slime-coated slabs near the top of the South Buttress, and mossy slabs low down on the descent.
The 65-degree notch on the old standard south-ridge line, and the short awkward step on the east-basin variation, which iced up and stopped a whole party in January.
No water on the entire route once the snow melts, on a full south aspect.
Slide alder, salal and dense young timber; one party's route through the burn-affected lower zone included heavy deadfall.
6,000 ft of steep trackless descent — the accumulated fatigue is a real hazard, not a figure of speech.

approach_variants.name: Fryingpan Creek, Summerland and Meany Crest to Whitman Notch
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Fryingpan Creek Trailhead near 3,800-3,900 ft on the Sunrise and White River Road, a few miles past the White River entrance station. Follow the signed trail up through old-growth beside Fryingpan Creek.

At roughly 3.2 miles and about 1,400 ft of gain there is an established footlog crossing of Fryingpan Creek — the main water and a spot that needs care in high runoff. Continue to Summerland at about 4.5 miles and roughly 5,900 ft: patrol cabin, pit toilet, bear wires, and the last reliable running water.

From Summerland leave maintained trail and take the climbers' path northwest of the campground knoll, up steep tundra and snow on the Meany Snowfield to Meany Crest, a rock outcrop at roughly 7,350-7,500 ft with flat sites and stone wind breaks. This is the standard high camp.

Above Meany Crest gain the toe of the Fryingpan Glacier and rope up. Climb south and southwest across the lower apron to the broad notch between the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers at about 9,000-9,100 ft, then traverse and climb the upper Whitman across a bergschrund to about 10,500-11,000 ft, where snow gives way to rock.

The basin holds heavy snow and the approach slopes can be avalanche terrain in soft early-season conditions. Afternoon whiteout and thunderstorm activity is common on Rainier's flanks.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun through Aug, best early July to early August — firm morning snow, drier rock, and bridges not yet melted out
hazards: Loose volcanic rock and rockfall on the summit gully and crest, worsening through the day
Crevasses and weakening bridges on the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers, worst in August and September
A bergschrund that is a step-across early season and a problem late
Cliff-out potential between Summerland and Meany Crest if the line drifts climber's right
Avalanche potential on the Meany Snowfield in soft or early-season conditions
Major exposure on the final crest, with about 2,000 ft to the Emmons on the north side
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Whitman Notch at about 9,100 ft is the arrival, and you know it by what becomes visible rather than by the altimeter: it is the first place the Whitman Glacier comes into view. Until you can see a second glacier on the far side, you have not reached the notch.

The base of the climbing proper is higher still, and it is a change of surface: at about 10,500-11,000 ft the snow ends and a loose rock-and-scree gully begins. That transition is the base. The sequence above it is countable and in this order: gully, a short step of about 6 ft, a gully-chimney, the summit notch, then an exposed scramble along the crest.

The route-finding trap is low, not high, and it is the one thing on this climb that regularly commits parties to bad ground: between Summerland and Meany Crest, if you find yourself contouring climber's right into a bowl under rock bands, you are cliffed out and off the line. The cairned and boot-packed line stays left of that bowl. Fix this by going back to the last cairn, not by traversing further.

The summit-crest test is a negative and it is unambiguous: the last 30 to 100 ft is a narrow crumbling andesite crest with roughly 2,000 ft dropping away to the Emmons Glacier on the north side. If the ground is not falling away on both sides of you, you have not reached the true summit — you are on the notch or a subsidiary block below it.

Timing as a finding: the andesite loosens as the sun works on it, and the crevasse bridges soften through the day. Being at the notch early is not tidiness, it is the whole plan.

approach_variants.name: White River Campground and the Wonderland Trail to Summerland

bivy.name: Meany Crest
bivy.notes: The standard high camp for Little Tahoma, and the one that makes the climb reasonable. It is a large flat area within the cliff band directly above Summerland, gained by the climbers' path and scrambling out of the basin, and it also serves Whitman Crest and the spires on that shoulder. From here the Fryingpan Glacier lies immediately ahead and the summit is a manageable morning rather than an epic. It is exposed — the shelf catches wind off the mountain and there is nothing to hide behind — so build walls if the forecast is doubtful and site the tent where a rockfall from the band above cannot reach it. Getting a permit for the zone is generally far easier than getting one of Summerland's few designated sites, which is a second, practical reason to camp high.
bivy.water: Meltwater runnels and small falls at the edge of the snow through most of the season — parties routinely find running water a short walk from camp. Late in a dry summer it thins out, so carry a stove and be prepared to melt
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit issued for the cross-country zone rather than a named site, obtained the same way and at the same per-person nightly rate as an established camp. Zone rules govern the pitch: well back from trails, at least a hundred feet from water, and on snow, rock or bare durable ground — never on the meadow. The climbing cost-recovery fee applies to this trip regardless of where you sleep, since the route crosses glaciers. There is no toilet, so human waste must be packed out; the park's blue bag system exists for exactly this and is the expected practice on any glaciated route here.
bivy.capacity: A broad, flat rock and snow shelf with room for several tents; no designated sites, no numbers, and no facilities

bivy.name: Summerland Camp
bivy.notes: The subalpine meadow basin that everything on this side of the mountain stages from, a little over four miles up the Wonderland Trail from the Fryingpan Creek bridge. For Little Tahoma it is the lower of the two realistic camps and much the more comfortable one — running water, a toilet, a stone shelter to cook under in bad weather, and a designated pitch. The catch is the site count and the competition: these are among the most sought-after backcountry sites in the park and they book out for midsummer weekends, with Wonderland Trail through-hikers taking most of them. Early season, before the Wonderland traffic builds, is when a climbing party can most easily get in. Camping here rather than higher costs you roughly 1,600 feet and a cliff band on summit morning, which turns Little Tahoma into a genuinely long day, so most parties treat Summerland as a staging night rather than a high camp.
bivy.water: Fryingpan Creek runs through the meadow just below the shelter and is reliable all season; treat it
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness permit, required for every overnight. In 2026 that is roughly twelve dollars per person per night for anyone sixteen and over, plus a per-trip application fee, booked through the federal reservation system with about two thirds of capacity reservable in advance and the rest held for walk-ups; walk-up permits are issued in person at the White River Wilderness Information Center on this side of the park, or at Longmire or Carbon River. The park's separate climbing cost-recovery fee — about eighty-two dollars a head — is NOT triggered by camping here, but IS triggered the moment you step onto the Fryingpan or Whitman Glacier, or go above 10,000 feet, which every route on Little Tahoma does. Pay it online before you arrive and bring proof; a climbing permit will not be issued to a team until every member has paid.
bivy.capacity: A handful of designated individual sites — around five — plus a stone shelter built by the Civilian Conservation Corps a little below them, and a backcountry toilet

bivy.name: Toe of the Fryingpan Glacier
bivy.notes: A slightly higher and more committed alternative to Meany Crest, on the moraine and snow where the Fryingpan Glacier begins. It shaves a little more off summit morning and puts you on the ice within minutes of leaving the tent, which is worth something on a route where the Whitman Glacier softens badly through the day and the descent is best done before it does. The ground is rubble and old ice rather than a shelf, so expect to build a platform, and expect the good spots to have moved since whatever description you read. The glacier here has been retreating steadily, which is the honest caveat: this camp is described differently in accounts a decade apart, and its condition should be treated as a current-season question rather than settled.
bivy.water: Glacial meltwater at the snout in warm weather, silty and worth settling before filtering, or snow to melt. Carry fuel on the assumption you will be melting
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone wilderness permit, same as Meany Crest. The climbing cost-recovery fee is unavoidable at this point — you are camping at the edge of a glacier. Pack out all human waste; there are no facilities above Summerland at all.
bivy.capacity: A small number of parties on moraine and snow at the glacier's lower edge; informal, and the usable ground shifts as the ice recedes

bivy.name: Whitman Glacier notch camp
bivy.notes: The highest of the three camps, in the prominent gap on the crest between the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers, just under the base of the peak itself. It reduces summit day to a short glacier walk and the East Shoulder scramble, which is its whole justification. Everything else about it is a cost: it is cold, wind-hammered, waterless, and small enough that a third party arriving has nowhere to go. Little Tahoma's summit block is notoriously loose volcanic rock and the peak is the site of one of the largest rockfalls recorded in the range, so where you site a tent relative to the slopes above matters more here than anywhere lower on the route. Sound judgement is to camp high only if the freezing level is low enough to keep the mountain frozen overnight.
bivy.water: Snow only. No running water at this elevation — carry all fuel for the bivouac and for summit day
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone wilderness permit, plus the climbing cost-recovery fee, which is mandatory here in every sense. Registration for the climb is completed in person at a wilderness information center before you start, and the climbing rangers' account of current glacier and rockfall conditions is worth treating as part of the plan rather than a formality. Blue bags for all waste.
bivy.capacity: Two or three tents in the gap, dug into snow; very limited and fully exposed

approach_variants.notes: The Fryingpan Creek trailhead and its spur trail are closed for the bridge replacement, planned to last into 2029. Park at White River Campground, where parking is limited, and follow the Wonderland Trail to Summerland. From Summerland the climb is unchanged: the climbers' path to Meany Crest, the Fryingpan Glacier and Whitman Notch.

approach_variants.name: From Paradise across the Cowlitz and Ingraham glaciers
approach_variants.notes: The usual way in winter and early season, before the Sunrise road opens. Climb toward Camp Muir to about 8,600 ft, traverse east across the Paradise and Cowlitz glaciers, through the Cathedral Rocks notch and across the Ingraham to the upper Whitman Glacier. Expect roughly 7 miles of glacier and snow travel to the base of the upper face.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack ford and Easy Ridge over the Imperfect Impasse to Perfect Pass
approach_variants.notes:
From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of Hannegan Pass Road, FS-32, off SR-542 at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 runs about 4 miles and 2,000 ft to Hannegan Pass at roughly 5,050-5,100 ft. The trail then switchbacks down the far side into the Chilliwack River valley to Boundary Camp and continues down-valley to the Chilliwack River crossing.

That ford is the approach's main hazard: it can be thigh-deep and swift at mid-summer flow, and is harder earlier in the season or after rain. From the ford, leave the maintained trail system and pick up the old, unmaintained Easy Ridge climbers' trail, which climbs steeply out of the valley to Easy Saddle at about 5,200 ft, a common camp, roughly 5.5 to 8.5 hours and 8-9 miles in depending on pace and the ford.

From Easy Saddle the route follows the crest over or around Easy Peak at 6,613 ft to the Imperfect Impasse, then continues to Perfect Pass at about 6,200 ft, the standard high camp, about 16 miles in, commonly the end of a second day, though fast parties reach it in one. There is no reliable water at Perfect Pass in late season; fill at Easy Saddle or from snowmelt.
hazards: A thigh-deep, swift ford of the Chilliwack River at mid-summer flow
The Imperfect Impasse: snow moats, wet down-sloping slabs, and an 800 ft descent to an exposed class 4 step as the workaround
Moats where the south snowfield meets the summit rock, worse late season
A short but very exposed summit crest on poor rock with limited protection
No reliable water at Perfect Pass in late season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The route starts where the camp ends: from Perfect Pass, head north and up onto the broad south snowfield. That snowfield is the lower margin of the Whatcom Glacier, the angle is moderate, and the line aims at a conspicuous col in the summit ridge above. Reports describe it as long but straightforward, roughly an hour from the pass.

So the aiming point is a notch in a skyline, and in cloud the substitute for it is this: keep climbing snow at a moderate angle until the snow runs out against rock. The snowfield is left at the col. Where snow meets rock is where a moat or a lip of hard snow is most likely to be awkward, and it is worse late in the season, which is exactly why you will notice it.

Confirm above: the final stretch along the crest is short, on the order of a hundred feet, but very exposed with drops on both sides, on poor rock with limited protection. Many parties belay it even though the moves are only third to fourth class. If you are on a long ridge rather than a hundred-foot one, you are not on this route.

The variation that is not an error: some parties break out onto ramps and ledges to the northeast of the col and rejoin the crest higher. Both reach the same place.

The impasse, which is the other thing you have to find on this approach: it is a notch guarded by deep snow moats on both sides and down-sloping, often wet slabs. In many seasons the direct crossing is unsafe or impassable; the established workaround drops roughly 800 ft to about 4,400 ft and re-climbs an exposed class 4 rock step, which many parties belay, to regain the ridge on the far side. Dropping 800 ft to get past a notch feels wrong and is correct.

approach_variants.name: The low-orbit traverse from Whatcom Pass, skipping Easy Ridge and the Impasse entirely
approach_variants.notes: An alternative that avoids the Impasse. From Whatcom Pass, reached via the Chilliwack River and Brush Creek trails or via the Little Beaver Creek Trail from Ross Lake, a low-orbit traverse around Whatcom Peak's east side on scree and snow reaches the same south-side snowfields.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; treat as glacier travel in early season
hazards: Moats and possible crevasses at the edge of the Whatcom Glacier; treat as glacier travel in early season
Scree and snow sidehilling with no path
The same summit crest exposure as the Easy Ridge variant
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This variant is defined by what it avoids, and that is the test: if you have crossed the impasse, you are not on it. The low orbit contours around the peak's east side instead of over the ridge crest, and delivers you onto the same south-side snowfields the Easy Ridge line reaches from Perfect Pass.

Arrival is the same arrival: broad moderate snow below a conspicuous col in the summit ridge, and the route is where the snow runs out against rock.

What you trade for it, and why the choice is a conditions call rather than a preference: the low orbit exposes you to the moats and possible crevasses at the edge of the Whatcom Glacier, so it should be treated as glacier travel with a rope and crevasse-rescue gear in early season. The Impasse is a rock problem; this is a glacier problem. Pick the one your party is equipped for.

wa_whitehorse_mountain_nw_shoulder.beta: Begin on Niederprum Trail #953/653, which quickly degenerates into a steep, brushy boot path gaining roughly 4,000 ft to an alpine bench near the old Niederprum mine. Continue on snow to Lone Tree Pass (~4,900 ft; the 'lone tree' is actually a cluster of three trees, not at the pass), traverse below the northwest ridge to High Pass (~6,000-6,030 ft), cross onto the Whitehorse Glacier, and climb a snow/ice ridge to the base of the summit block, finishing with exposed Class 3 scrambling to the true summit.
watch_out: The moat/bergschrund below the summit rock is easy to underestimate — carry a picket and be ready to belay it
Snow conditions in the couloir and on the glacier change fast through the day; an early start is essential, not optional
Beyond the maintained 1.4 miles of Trail #653, the path can vanish into brush — only experienced route-finders should continue

wa_bears_breast_mountain_infinite_beauty.approach: From the Salmon La Sac Trailhead, follow the Waptus River Trail and PCT about 9 miles to Waptus Lake and on to a camp near the Waptus River PCT bridge, roughly 11-12 flat miles one-way; from camp, the old track along Shovel Creek leads to the base of the Mega Slab, starting at its lowest point.
pro_tips: Start at the very lowest point of the slab on the shallow rib to stay on-route.
Most parties climb the bulk of the slab in trail runners or approach shoes and save rock shoes for the summit chimney.
This route sees roughly one party a year — the 12-mile approach, not the climbing, is the crux for most teams.

wa_pinnacle_peak_tatoosh_r1.beta: From Pinnacle-Plummer saddle, head east and scramble up obvious gullies on the peak's south side with multiple line options. Stay on most-traveled route for least loose rock. Route-finding is straightforward but exposure increases with altitude. Final push to summit is the steepest and most difficult section, with some variations described as low 5th class.
